synthesis.north_star: A platform an agent can hold in its head: every concept has one home, one name and one mechanism; every route, tool, flag and file earns its place through a live caller; retired things are deleted, not carried beside their replacement; and no simplification weakens a trust guarantee.

ranked_moves.payoff: -4,896 lines and one CI step pair; -165k lines / 2,024 files, a 372-LOC guard, its 525-LOC test and a 183 KB baseline; about 1.5 MB of stale changes.
ranked_moves.outcome: The committed COPY_INVENTORY.md and its CI/Makefile guard go (generator stays on demand); each of the 579 baseline entries is decided (landed, re-filed as a bead, or dropped by the owner) before openspec/changes/archive and its guard are deleted; about 16 unreferenced active changes and zero-citer plan files are removed.
ranked_moves.non_goals: No live-spec rewrite; no change to the OpenSpec workflow itself (an owner decision); never delete the archive before the 579 are triaged.
ranked_moves.governing_intent: about/craft-and-care/review-and-documentation.md Document Lifecycle ('moving the same body to an archive is not consolidation; git history preserves the removed body'); run-18 north star (one home, one name, one mechanism; retired things are deleted, not carried; simplicity never weakens trust).

measure-complexity.summary: The platform's complexity is not spread evenly. It sits in a few very large files and in concepts that have several names or homes. Two functions hold more cyclomatic complexity than whole butlers: Spawner._run has CC 301 over 2,332 lines, and MessagePipeline.process has CC 244 over 2,027 lines. Calendar is the largest feature family at 37k LOC, with a provider ABC that has one implementation. The most-churned code file is a hand-written frontend copy of the backend models (types.ts: 10.6k LOC, 158 commits in 90 days, 136 of them also touching backend Python). Roster code is reached through five naming schemes plus 22 ad-hoc file loaders. Butler-specific scheduled jobs have two homes (src/butlers/jobs and roster/<b>/jobs) and are wired through 100 hand-written core wrappers. Google token refresh is reimplemented at 13 sites, and only 2 files use the shared revocation classifier. The import graph has no layering: 28 subsystem pairs import each other, core imports the API layer at 5 sites, and src has 56 import edges into specific butlers. The simplest honest design keeps each of these as one concept with one home and one mechanism. That means generated API types, roster-owned job t…

runtime-core.summary: Today a butler starts work in eight ways: the trigger tool, route.execute, startup route-inbox recovery, scheduler cron prompts, deterministic jobs, deadline/event-chain/deferred-notify passes, QA dispatch and memory consolidation. That makes 7 live Spawner.trigger call sites in 6 files, plus a dead eighth in healing/dispatch.py. The dashboard API also runs a second job model alongside scheduled_tasks: 9 supervised lifespan loops, 7 with env-var intervals. The daemon's state is split across ButlerDaemon (46 attributes, 60 private attributes touched from other files through `daemon: Any` helpers), process-global registries keyed by pool id or butler name, and 6 ContextVars that inject ambient dependencies into jobs. The one good convergence is scheduled_tasks: delegation and domain-event wakes already become one-shot tasks there. The simplest honest design keeps that table as the only job model. It would have one route-execution function shared by live and recovered routes, one declarative job table validated at startup, and one model-failover helper, and it would delete the dead healing dispatch chain, the per-tick schema probes and the trigger that cannot fire. The duplication is…

ledger_feedback.note: Under-scoped direction: it proposes a new 6-state job-health projection plus transition history for the 9 supervise_lifespan_loop loops in api/app.py. That would be a third job-state mechanism beside scheduled_tasks (next_run_at/last_run_at) and infra_conditions. Prefer giving those loops the scheduled_tasks row shape (cron, last_run_at, last_result) in a public control-plane table, so there is one job model and one schedule UI.

trust-machinery.summary: Today, one Postgres login (POSTGRES_USER from the shared butlers.postgresEnv helper) runs the migrations, dashboard-api and the butler daemons, and it owns every Alembic-created table. On top of that, init-db.sql grants blanket DML on every public table to all 14 runtime roles. Because the baseline grants too much, each narrow guarantee (DND single writer, runtime-attention outbox, restore-drill evidence) has had to be built as its own bunker inside scripts/init-db.sql. The pattern is the same each time: a purpose NOLOGIN owner, an *_admin schema, a bootstrap_configuration singleton, install/finalize/rollback SECURITY DEFINER interfaces, and, for runtime attention, a v2-v5 upgrade/deactivate ladder that works as a second migration framework. Nothing in deploy/ re-runs that file, so a runtime diagnostic (stored_function_drift.py) regex-parses init-db.sql to detect drift, and about 3k lines of tests pin its text. The file grew from about 700 to 5,832 lines in two months (22 commits, +5,115/-508). The simplest honest design uses three separate logins: a migrator that owns objects, one runtime login per process that can SET ROLE only to its own role, and the bootstrap superuser. Publi…

grades.reason: Three hand-built bunkers with their own install/finalize/rollback and version ladders. The file is applied only by hand and is checked by regex-parsing its text.
Per-butler SET ROLE exists. But one login owns all tables and can RESET ROLE, and under the default dev posture a failed role check silently runs with shared privileges.
Blanket DML default for all 14 runtime roles. Every narrow guarantee is a REVOKE/RLS/definer exception that init-db re-widens on rerun (bu-yfd9v1).
Many container-backed behaviour tests exist, but thousands of lines pin SQL and doc text instead of probing catalog behaviour.

ledger_feedback.note: Under-scoped: reviewing public tables one at a time cannot persist while init-db.sql:464 re-grants blanket DML on every rerun. The fix is to flip the default to deny and add a declarative grant manifest (move 2). Then bu-w24vr3 (qa_patrols forgeable) closes as one manifest row.

BYPASSRLS hardening matters only because FORCE RLS on public.user_context is the DND boundary. If DND authority becomes a plain table GRANT under move 2, the remaining risk is mostly table ownership by the shared login (move 1), which RLS cannot fix.

The contacts backfill is one of 18 core files that run SQL on relationship.* from arbitrary host roles. Fixing contacts alone leaves the same failure class in memory/tools/writing.py, approvals/email_guard.py, gmail_policy.py, api/routers/contacts.py and others. A ratchet is needed (move 5).

Porting the Docker/iptables/boot_id executor to k8s carries ~9.6k LOC and 3 privileged roles forward. Restoring into an ephemeral Postgres pod needs no privilege on the live cluster and lets the init-db restore-drill section be deleted (move 4).
'Fix the CREATEDB grant' assumes the drill restores inside the live cluster. An out-of-cluster ephemeral target removes CREATEDB from every role in the live cluster.

The compose-vs-Helm split also leaves BUTLERS_POSTURE (compose-only) controlling whether schema isolation fails closed. Helm never sets it, so k3s runs fail-open. Deleting posture (move 3) removes one axis of this reconciliation.

data-model.summary: Today the database is described by 416 migration files (59.6k LOC: 230 core revisions plus 12 roster chains and 5 module chains), plus 5,832 lines of privileged scripts/init-db.sql. That bootstrap is a second DDL and upgrade home: 8 public tables, 4 admin tables, 42 functions and 114 GRANT/REVOKE statements. Each of the 13 daemons replays the core chain into its own schema at startup (lifecycle.py:146-149). Yet 57 core files create database-global public/connectors/dashboard_auth tables, so those files must be written to be idempotent across 13 replays, and 9 of them hard-code a list of butler schemas. One P1 nightly failure (bu-u20z6z) exists only because of this replay-across-bootstrap shape. Ownership is uneven. The calendar module declares no migrations, but its 9 tables live in core and land in all 13 schemas when only 7 butlers enable calendar. One concept also has parallel homes: audit (public.audit_log plus a write-only switchboard.operator_audit_log), outbox/delivery (4 mechanisms) and credentials (3 homes). The simplest honest design has one public chain run once and one per-butler core chain. Each chain, roster and module alike, is squashed to a baseline proven equal to…

ledger_feedback.note: The failing assertion tests a downgrade/upgrade replay of core_258 across the managed bootstrap. That scenario exists only because the core chain replays global DDL per schema and supports downgrade below current head. A re-baseline (data-model move 1) deletes the subject, so do not spend more P1 coordinator time beyond deciding whether to re-baseline.

'Drop core_265 conversation-identity snapshot tables after soak': there is no production deployment, so there is nothing to soak. The 3 backup tables (core_265_conversation_identity_split.py:88-92) can go now, or simply be absent from a baseline.

Template cloning amortizes replay but still builds each template by replaying 416 migrations into 13 schemas. A baseline shrinks the template build and its catalog becomes the baseline's equality oracle. Sequence: land .8 first, then validate the baseline against the same template's catalog.

Its 'catalog snapshot' is the oracle a migration squash needs. Scope it to cover all 13 butler schemas plus public/dashboard_auth/connectors, including grants, RLS policies, definer ownership/search_path and triggers, so it can certify a baseline as catalog-equal.

architecture.md:59-61 says cross-schema read exceptions must be 'auditable via migration history'. A squash removes that history, so the planned cross-schema read-exception register must become the audit home and the doctrine wording must change in the same PR.

Systematic review of public-table write access: after a public-once chain split, the grant surface to review is one baseline file plus init-db, instead of 180 core files written for 13 replays. Do the split first or the review goes stale.

connector-family.summary: The connectors package has 41 entries and 49.0k LOC. It ships 13 connector processes: 12 in Helm and live_listener in compose only. The shared plumbing is mostly adopted already: cursor_store, heartbeat, mcp_client, metrics and health_socket are used by 13 or 14 of 14 connectors, and Helm already uses one generic Deployment template. The complexity sits around that core. (1) A connector's identity (type, channel, provider) is hand-kept in about 10 separate lists that disagree with each other: the dashboard's /available catalog differs from the deployed values for 9 of 13 connectors. Meanwhile CONNECTOR_CHANNEL and CONNECTOR_PROVIDER are env-configurable even though the routing contract fixes them, and 4 connectors ignore those env vars entirely. (2) The Google family repeats the same transport: 10 hand-written refresh-token mint functions (about 870 LOC) and 3 copies of a multi-account supervisor (about 1.3k LOC). (3) Spotify and Home Assistant each have two clients for the same API, one in the connector and one in the butler module. (4) Discord was retired in v1.md by owner decision (2026-10-04), yet its 1.4k-LOC connector, its pyproject script and the dashboard's "available" lis…

messaging-delivery.summary: Inbound traffic mostly converges already: connectors, dashboard chat (conversations.py:350 calls Switchboard `ingest`), delegation and domain-event fan-out all reach a butler through Switchboard route() and route.execute into route_inbox. Telegram one-tap callbacks are the exception: three separate handlers inside the telegram_bot connector deal with them. Outbound is where the complexity sits. I count 9 parallel paths to the owner: the notify() MCP tool, quiet-hours deferred_notifications, the insight broker digest, the runtime_attention_outbox worker, the legacy approval push, a dark RFC 0023 approval-intent pipeline, decision_routing via decision_prompts, deterministic jobs and connectors that build notify.v1 themselves, and Chronicler sending straight to the Telegram Bot API. All of them except the last end at Switchboard `deliver()`, which wraps notify.v1 inside route.v1 and sends it to Messenger. On Messenger the core route.execute takes a synchronous branch, keyed on the butler name, that sends through its telegram, email and whatsapp modules. The simplest honest design: (1) one owner-notify function in core that builds the envelope, applies posture and quiet-hours checks, …

frontend-surface.summary: The frontend is cleaner than its size suggests: knip finds zero unused files, there are 50 shell capabilities in one manifest (lib/shell-capability.ts) that already drives router, rail, finder and prefetch, and data access is almost entirely react-query hooks over one client. The weight is elsewhere: 49% of the 332k LOC is tests; API shape lives in two hand-maintained homes (10.6k-line api/types.ts plus a 1,333-line Python test that regex-parses client.ts) plus a third 1,295-line barrel; a 2,050-line single-rule ESLint plugin guards one CSS-variable family; 14 legacy redirect routes have zero internal callers; and tiny primitives (empty/error/loading lines, tile skeletons, KPI cells, duration formatters) are re-declared 5-11 times beside a shared kit. The simplest honest design keeps every page with a live owner capability, gives each API shape one home (the OpenAPI schema), gives each primitive one definition, lets a butler with a first-class page skip a duplicate in-detail tab, and replaces AST-grade lint and a 4.9k-line committed generated inventory with cheap checks.

dashboard-api.summary: Today the dashboard API serves 618 OpenAPI operations (535 paths, 1,094 component schemas) from 61 core router files plus 13 auto-discovered roster routers. 501 operations have a frontend caller and 20 more are called by the daemon, OAuth or Telegram. 96 operations (15.5%, about 5.3k handler LOC) have no caller anywhere. They include whole dead routers (v1 secrets, module-states, provider settings), a second approval-decision family with weaker actor attribution, and routes that can only ever return 409 or 503. Each wire shape lives twice: the Pydantic models, then 850 hand-written TypeScript types (432 share a name with an OpenAPI schema). A 1,333-LOC TypeScript fragment parser checks only paths and query names between the two copies. Envelopes come in four wrapper types plus 202 unwrapped routes. There are 14 near-identical cursor codecs, and 63 degraded-flag field names (five of them different names for "list of failed sources"). The simplest honest design: every route has a live caller or is deleted. Each decision has one path. Frontend wire types are generated from create_app().openapi(), so Pydantic is the only home of a shape and caller drift is checked by tsc. A single lis…

config-and-deploy.summary: Today a single setting often has several homes, several names, or none that anyone sets. Non-test code reads at least 164 distinct env vars, and 96 of them appear in no deploy file. In k8s only Helm-rendered env reaches pods, so at least 59 tuning knobs always run at their code defaults. Each connector's identity (provider, channel, health port, log dir) is declared in Helm, in compose, in the connector's own constants, in a heartbeat allow-list, in the switchboard contract literals and in the dashboard catalog, and the spellings drift. The 13 butler.toml files restate code defaults (db name and schema, switchboard URL, three registration-only seed keys), and the loader silently ignores misspelled keys. Three deploy mechanisms exist side by side: Helm `make ship-*`, `scripts/compose.sh` and the compose-based `butlers deploy` verb. The simplest honest design: Helm is the only deploy path; anything that is a fact about a connector or butler is a code constant; butler.toml holds only what really differs per butler and is checked against a strict schema that rejects unknown keys; env carries only site facts and secrets (one public base URL, DB host, OTEL endpoint); a flag is deleted o…

The decision should end in deleting the compose-based `butlers deploy` verb (core/deploy.py 957 LOC, cli.py deploy command, tests/core/test_deploy.py 994, tests/cli/test_cli_deploy.py 175) and compose.sh --prod, with helm deploys recording to public.deployments (bu-viat6h.5), not just reconciling the topology doc.

live_listener (4,348 LOC, 14 never-set env knobs) runs only under the compose --audio profile and has no helm entry, so retiring compose leaves voice with no runtime. The scope decision should say explicitly whether voice gets a helm entry or is retired.

The connector kit should also own connector settings: one env loader (gmail.py carries two, at 414-573 and 3469), identity constants instead of CONNECTOR_PROVIDER/CHANNEL env, and one default health port. Otherwise the kit consolidates mechanisms but leaves the knob sprawl in place.

observability-ops.summary: Today every signal kind has two to four sinks, and each reader is wired to a different one. App logs go to stdout, per-butler and uvicorn rotating JSON files, and a per-schema butler_logs table; the dashboard Logs tab reads only the table, the QA log_scanner reads only the files, and the table has no retention row. Metrics use two libraries: OTel over OTLP in daemons, and prometheus_client in connectors plus 19 definitions in daemon/API processes that no endpoint serves. Dashboard Prometheus reads (core/prometheus.py, PROMETHEUS_URL) are set by no tracked deploy config, and the ingestion funnel queries four series that no code emits. Liveness has a legacy HTTP POST path kept behind a flag, an MCP keepalive loop, connector heartbeats and the receiver-derived observer. The 2026-10-11 symptoms are the same pattern: bu-hc9n55 is a hard-coded schema list in core_089 that missed concierge (core_090 had already patched chronicler the same way), and bu-yq0rz9 is a daemon-to-dashboard HTTP edge that outlived the auth model and is now kept for rollback. The simplest honest design is one emission path (structured stdout), one durable queryable error store (butler_logs at WARN+ with a retenti…

knowledge-sprawl.summary: The normative corpus is not mostly normative: tracked markdown is 372,611 lines in 2,896 files, more than src/butlers code (341k LOC), and 164,720 lines (44%; 10.5 MB, 2,024 files) sit in openspec/changes/archive. That copy carries no live authority, and docs/roadmap/openspec-overview.md says "an archive directory is not proof that its requirements reached the baseline". The "40 MB" openspec figure is du disk blocks. Real bytes are 18.2 MB: archive 10.5, specs 4.0, active changes 3.7. Live-spec prose, docs and about are nearly disjoint (0.1-0.4% shared 10-word shingles), and file-path references in docs, about and specs are healthy. So the live knowledge tree is mostly not duplicated or stale; the sprawl is the archive and the machinery built to police it. The simplest honest design is that git history is the archive: landing a change applies its delta to openspec/specs and deletes the change directory, the archived-requirements guard moves from a standing 579-entry ratchet to a check on the PR that deletes a change, and a new feature gets one spec-delta home instead of RFC plus proposal plus design plus tasks plus plan plus bead. That would remove roughly 165k lines of markdown, …

deep-target-architecture.summary: Target end state: eight layers, each concept in one home. (1) Transport: connectors/ holds runnable connectors, the bu-ly3lv5.14 kit (submit_ingest/create_connector_pool/serve_health) and a single ConnectorDescriptor table. Helm values, heartbeat, bearer-scrub labels, OAuth scope rows, switchboard channel literals and the dashboard catalog are all derived from that table. (2) Ingress/routing: Switchboard ingest -> route() -> one execute_route_row(mode=live|recovered) over route_inbox. The pipeline is switchboard wiring, not a module, and Messenger owns its deliver executor. (3) Butler runtime: ButlerDaemon has one way into Spawner.trigger per work kind, and one scheduler resolves every job from declarations next to their owners (Module.jobs() plus roster/<b>/jobs JOBS). There is no central per-butler handler map. (4) Capabilities: the Module ABC has defaulted members, one loader, and tools/migrations/lifecycle plus declared jobs. (5) Delivery: one notify.v1 builder and one Switchboard transport. The outbox follows the owner's RFC 0023 decision. (6) Data: per-butler schema plus public (data-model/trust lenses own this). (7) Control surface: dashboard-api keeps only routes with call…

critic.summary: The harvest has all 16 lenses, so none is missing. I tried to falsify its ten boldest claims against source. The deletion claims mostly hold. Four moves weaken a trust guarantee as written and need the fixes listed in findings: the DND part of deny-by-default, the operator-audit fold, Messenger's direct deliver tool, and deleting the openspec archive. Two moves ride on settings that are not settled: the liveness cutover flag and the Discord owner decision. The end state I propose: one owner login per process and deny-by-default grants (trust-machinery moves 1-2) become the only cross-process trust mechanism. Machinery that adds a second private trust system on top of a database login every process shares is then re-justified or folded onto those grants. The first case is the runtime-probe capability plane, which no lens mentions: 2,236 src LOC plus 10,884 LOC across 20 test files, an Ed25519 keyring in BWS, Helm mounts and a receipts table. Retired code is caught by a ratchet that flags production symbols whose only callers are tests (67 such functions, 1,331 LOC today), not only by one-off sweeps. deep-data-and-trust.summary: All four input lenses (data-model, trust-machinery, messaging-delivery, observability-ops) were in the harvest. I re-verified their load-bearing claims against source, and two of them needed correcting (see findings). The designed end state has three Postgres authorities. (1) A bootstrap superuser runs a short scripts/init-db.sql: preflight, extensions, NOLOGIN purpose roles, butler roles derived from the roster, schemas, and deny-by-default. (2) A migrator login exists only in the `db migrate` initContainer. It is the single migration runner: a public chain runs once, then one baselined core/butler/module chain per schema, checked against today's catalog by an equality oracle. It owns every object and applies one roster-derived grant manifest. Every SECURITY DEFINER lives in an ordinary Alembic revision, owned by a purpose NOLOGIN role with a pinned search_path. (3) Runtime logins (butlers-up, connectors, cronjobs, dashboard) own nothing. They SET ROLE fail-closed and pass a connect-time reach assertion generalised from owner_auth. Because they own nothing, immutability triggers, RLS and definers can no longer be disabled or altered by runtime code. As a result the three *_admin …

findings.title: REFINEMENT: 'one runtime login per process' does not give per-butler isolation, because one process hosts all 13 butlers

Today one login migrates, serves the dashboard and runs the daemons, and init-db.sql:802-805 names that as the reason for three bespoke *_admin bunkers. ledger_feedback.note: Recording the privileged dashboard-api as accepted posture is the wrong end state. The dashboard pool owns tables (api/db.py:90-102; control_plane_identity.py:177-180). Supersede it with authority move S3 (a dashboard login that owns nothing).

Under-scoped: a per-table review re-widens on every init-db rerun (init-db.sql:436/464). Re-scope as authority move S2 (roster-derived deny-by-default manifest plus catalog ACL diff); bu-w24vr3 and bu-3leptg become manifest rows.

Re-scope from 'port the restore-drill executor to k8s' to 'replace it with an ephemeral-Postgres CronJob that writes one writer-attested audit row'; that deletes the executor, firewall, proxy, core_196 and the restore_drill_executor bunker instead of porting them.

Build its catalog snapshot to include owners, relacl, pg_policy, pg_trigger and pg_proc prosecdef/proconfig/proacl, so the same oracle proves both the baseline squash (migration move S3) and the grant manifest (authority move S2).
The replay-inventory failure class disappears once the public chain runs once (migration move S2); limit the work to unblocking the nightly run, not hardening the replay.
BYPASSRLS normalisation belongs in the single init-db role block and in catalog test (a) of the authority move; it is not a separate mechanism.
Fold into the generic definer catalog test (every prosecdef has a pinned search_path) instead of a per-RFC edit.
